explicacion.en: Importar means “to matter, to bother”. Sí means “Yes, it bothers me”. To say you don't mind, answer No, claro que no.

titulo.en: Asking for favors with tú and usted

texto.en: In Spanish you usually ask for a favor with a question, not with an order. With a friend (tú): ¿Me prestas tu cargador? means “Can you lend me your charger?”, which is how Spanish says “Can I borrow your charger?”. Prestar means “to lend”, so you ask the other person to lend it to you; me means “to me”. For help, use ¿Me puedes + infinitive?: ¿Me puedes ayudar? means “Can you help me?”. Only poder changes; the second verb stays in the infinitive. To ask “Do you mind…?” use ¿Te importa + infinitive?: ¿Te importa cerrar la ventana? (the stress falls on por: eem-POR-tah). Be careful with the answer: No, claro que no means “No, of course not”, that is, “I don't mind, no problem”. Sí, me importa means “Yes, I mind”. With a neighbor or an older person (usted) the verb changes: ¿Me presta…? ¿Me puede ayudar? ¿Le importa abrir la puerta? A direct order such as Abre la ventana, por favor is also possible with a friend, but a question sounds softer and more polite.
The same favors in two registers. Tap each phrase to hear it.

titulo.en: Do you want me to help you?

objetivo.en: Offer help with ¿te ayudo?, ¿le ayudo? and the fixed phrase ¿quieres que te ayude?, and answer an offer politely.

explicacion.en: After ¿Quieres que…? the verb has a special form: ayude, lleve, abra. It is not the usual present (ayudo). Learn the whole phrase for now.
With a neighbor or an older person, use usted: ¿Le ayudo? ¿Te ayudo? is for friends.

erroresFrecuentes.incorrecto: La caja es pesada. ¿Quieres que lo lleve?
erroresFrecuentes.correcto: La caja es pesada. ¿Quieres que la lleve?

explicacion.en: When the thing is la caja, the pronoun must agree: caja is feminine, so la. Lo is only for a masculine noun.

texto.en: To offer help, Spanish uses a short question in the present: ¿Te ayudo? to a friend (tú) and ¿Le ayudo? to a neighbor or an older person (usted). Both mean “Shall I help you?”. A longer, very common offer is ¿Quieres que te ayude? (tú) or ¿Quiere que le ayude? (usted): “Do you want me to help you?”. You can use the same formula with other actions: ¿Quieres que lo lleve? “Do you want me to carry it?” and ¿Quieres que abra la puerta? “Do you want me to open the door?”. For now, learn these phrases whole: the verb after que (ayude, lleve, abra) looks different from the present you know, and you will study why later. Use lo, la, los or las for the thing you carry: la caja → ¿Quieres que la lleve? Common answers: Sí, gracias. / Sí, por favor. / No, gracias, puedo yo (“No, thanks, I can do it myself”).
Short and long offers. Tap each phrase to hear it.

nota.en: Está prohibido + infinitive. On signs: Prohibido fumar.

explicacion.en: After puede the second verb stays in the infinitive: fumar. Only puede is conjugated, and it never changes in this question.
Where English uses -ing (“Smoking is forbidden”), Spanish uses the infinitive: Está prohibido fumar.

texto.en: To ask whether something is allowed, use ¿Se puede + infinitive?: ¿Se puede pintar la pared? means “Can one paint the wall?” or “Is it allowed to paint the wall?”. The question is about the rule, not about a specific person, so the form never changes: always se puede, never “se puedo” or “se puedes”. English often says “Can I…?” or “Can you…?”; Spanish uses se puede when the question is about what the rules allow. Answers: Sí, se puede. / No, no se puede. / Está prohibido + infinitive (“it is forbidden to…”). You can also hear Está permitido + infinitive (“it is allowed to…”). In Spanish the infinitive does the job of the English -ing form: Está prohibido fumar = “Smoking is forbidden”. On signs you only see Prohibido fumar.

explicacion.en: The rule “command = él form” does not work for venir. Use the short command: ven.
Hacer has an irregular tú command: haz. Hace is the present for él or ella.
The command of ser is sé, with an accent. Se without an accent is a different word.

texto.en: A regular command for tú (affirmative) looks like the él form of the present: lee, abre, escribe. Eight common verbs break this rule and have a short command of their own: poner → pon, venir → ven, hacer → haz, decir → di, salir → sal, tener → ten, ir → ve and ser → sé. Learn them as a group. Haz sounds like “ahs” (the z is an s). Sé has a written accent to tell it from se; di and ve have none. With pronouns, the pronoun attaches to the end: dímelo (“tell it to me”) and ponlo (“put it”). In dímelo the stress falls on the third syllable from the end, so it needs a written accent; in ponlo the stress falls on the second to last syllable and the word ends in a vowel, so it needs none. These are affirmative commands for tú. Negative commands are formed differently, and you will study them later. Use them with a friend or a teacher who asks you to use tú, like Sofía.
Tap each phrase to hear it. The usted command is a review.

titulo.en: Building rules: hay que and no se permite

texto.en: Rules do not say who has to do something. Spanish has fixed phrases for that. Hay que + infinitive means a general obligation: Hay que sacar la basura el lunes = “You have to take out the trash on Monday” (everyone has to). Hay que never changes. No se permite + infinitive means a formal prohibition: No se permite hacer ruido después de las diez = “Making noise is not allowed after ten”. Its opposite is Se permite + infinitive (“it is allowed”). You already know similar phrases: ¿Se puede…? asks if something is allowed, and Está prohibido… or Prohibido… appears on signs. Compare tener que, which says who: Tengo que sacar la basura (I have to). Hay que is for the rule in general.
Obligation, prohibition, permission. Tap each phrase to hear it.

explicacion.en: The rule “command = él form” does not work for venir. Use the short command: ven.
Hacer has an irregular tú command: haz. Hace is the present for él or ella.
The command of ser is sé, with an accent. Se without an accent is a different word.
